one_liner: Sandboxed C (or Python/Lua) web application server; outran an OpenResty nginx echo setup 1.5x in a 2015 unequal hello-world test.
what_it_does: Kore is an HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket application platform: you write request handlers in C (or Python, or Lua) and build them, with the kodev tool, into a module that Kore loads or into one standalone binary. It is not an nginx drop-in: it has its own configuration file, routing, parameter validation and optional asynchronous PostgreSQL, curl and background tasks, and it terminates TLS itself (on by default) with ACME certificate support.
how_it_is_fast: One single-threaded, edge-triggered event loop (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD and macOS) per worker process, workers pinned to CPUs by default, and a shared-memory compare-and-swap accept lock that each worker takes for a batch of new connections (worker_accept_threshold) so accepts are spread without a thundering herd. Requests and buffers come from fixed-size freelist pools (kore_pool), responses are queued as netbufs, files go out with sendfile, and TCP_NODELAY is set on accepted sockets.
when_to_use: A small, self-contained HTTP/1.1 or WebSocket API service written in C where you want TLS termination, privilege separation and seccomp/pledge sandboxing without a separate reverse proxy.
Embedded or appliance-style deployments on Linux, OpenBSD, FreeBSD or macOS (x64, arm, aarch64) that want a single binary with handlers compiled in.
Dynamic responses where per-request handler cost is low and you want one event loop per core; the 2015 test showed about 570k hello-world req/s on a 6-core Xeon E5-1650 v2.
Projects that want to mix C handlers with Python or Lua handlers and async PostgreSQL in one process model.
when_not_to_use: Serving static files or reverse proxying at scale: nginx (or H2O) is the incumbent there, and the only Kore-vs-nginx number compared a 4-worker nginx echo module against 12 Kore workers.
You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3: the README lists HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket only.
Windows or exotic architectures: only Linux, OpenBSD, FreeBSD and macOS on x64, arm and aarch64 are supported.

Teams that need a large ecosystem or a GitHub-based contribution flow: development is essentially one maintainer, patches go to a mailing list, and Kore is absent from the current the-benchmarker/web-frameworks suite (2026-10-06 data), so there is no recent third-party performance data.

integration.dependencies: OpenSSL 1.1.1/3 or LibreSSL 3.x (omit with TLS_BACKEND=none); optional libcurl 7.64+, pthreads (tasks), libpq (pgsql), Python 3.6+, Lua 5.4+
integration.platforms: Linux, OpenBSD, FreeBSD, macOS; x64, arm and aarch64 only
integration.thread_safety: Each worker is a single-threaded event-loop process; optional background tasks (TASKS=1) run on pthreads. No broader thread-safety guarantee is documented.

gotchas: Harness flaw beyond the known worker-count gap (nginx worker_processes 4 vs Kore workers 12 on a 12-thread CPU shared with 12 wrk threads): the responses were not equivalent. The benchmark handler calls http_response(req, 200, "Hello World", 12), so Kore sends a 12-byte body including the C string's NUL terminator, no Content-Type, and its 2.0-devel default server, keep-alive and strict-transport-security headers; nginx sent 'Hello World!' as text/html with Date and Server stripped. wrk's byte counts work out to about 191 bytes per Kore response vs about 119 for nginx (derived from the raw result files). Kore did more bytes, so this does not inflate its lead, but neither matches the suite's text/plain spec.

Compiler flags at the benchmarked Kore commit 4356c3e (2.0.0-devel) were -g with no -O flag in both the Makefile and the module build in cli.c, so unless the tester exported CFLAGS, Kore ran at GCC's default -O0; current Kore builds with -O2. Nginx's p50 latency (63-68 us) was actually lower than Kore's (122-127 us); only its p75 and higher (6.9-7.7 ms at p75, 22.5-28.7 ms at p99) were worse, consistent with 4 nginx workers being preempted by wrk threads.

HSTS is on by default (HTTP_HSTS_ENABLE 31536000) even in plain-HTTP builds; set http_hsts_enable 0 behind a TLS-terminating proxy. Worker CPU affinity is also on by default (worker_set_affinity 1), which can collide with container CPU limits.

Fixes land on master well after the last release (4.2.3): for example 'http: Make sure nb->s_off - len doesn't underflow' (2026-09-02) and a request-queue ordering fix (2026-10-03); several build flavors cannot be combined (README).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Kore over H2O, Lwan, libevhtp or Drogon when you want a C application server with built-in TLS, ACME, privilege separation and seccomp/pledge sandboxing rather than raw peak throughput; Lwan and H2O have stronger and newer performance evidence (TechEmpower, HTTP/2), and H2O or nginx are the better choice for static files and proxying.
verified_claims_summary: Third-party nanoant/WebFrameworkBenchmark (2015, Ubuntu 14.04, Xeon E5-1650 v2, wrk 12 threads and 100 keep-alive connections on the same host, best of four 20 s runs): Kore 2.0-devel built with make NOTLS=1 and 12 workers served 572,782 hello-world req/s vs 381,368 for OpenResty's nginx with the echo module and 4 workers, about 1.5x; Undertow (616,547) beat both. The worker counts, response headers and bodies differ, so the ratio is not like-for-like.
status_note: Actively maintained by its author (commits through 2026-10-03, ISC licence, 3.8k stars, release 4.2.3), with a security-first design, but performance evidence is a single 2015 third-party run against a deliberately small nginx configuration.
